summary:
The Last Signal is a cinematic, continuous-loop 3D interactive web expedition built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (“Abandoned, Not Forgotten”). It unifies Apollo lunar history, engineering, and extraterrestrial archaeology into a seamless, scroll-driven experience.

The journey opens on a July 16, 1969 newspaper broadsheet that match-cuts directly into Launch Complex 39A. As users scroll, the 363-foot Saturn V rocket launches with procedural F-1 flame plumes, atmospheric exhaust haze, and multistage separation into orbit. A relativistic lunar crater warp tunnel plunges the camera to the surface, revealing the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle in a staged, 7-assembly mechanical exploded breakdown with real-time telemetry badges.

Continuing across the regolith, visitors explore historic artifacts left behind: the operational Apollo 11 Laser Retroreflector (LRRR), the Passive Seismic Experiment, and the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle at Hadley–Apennine, before an orbital Earthrise smoothly loops back to the morning of launch.

Engineered with React Three Fiber, Three.js, GSAP ScrollTrigger, and Lenis inertia scrolling, the platform delivers 60 FPS performance, Draco-compressed 3D geometry, ACES Filmic lighting, and dynamic spatial audio without jarring cuts
details:
PROJECT DETAILS: THE LAST SIGNAL

Team: Quark Babies

Challenge: Abandoned, Not Forgotten — NASA International Space Apps Challenge

1. WHAT DOES IT DO OR HOW DOES IT WORK?

The Last Signal is an interactive, cinematic 3D web archive that chronicles humanity's extraterrestrial heritage on the Moon through a single, continuous, scroll-driven journey.

- Match-Cut Transition: It begins with an authentic July 16, 1969 newspaper broadsheet. As the user scrolls, the newspaper photograph zooms in and match-cuts smoothly into a real-time 3D reconstruction of Launch Complex 39A.

- Launch and Staging Simulation: Scrolling propels the 363-foot Saturn V rocket through liftoff, atmospheric ascent with custom flame and exhaust shaders, and sequential stage separations (S-IC, S-II, S-IVB) into Translunar Injection.

- Relativistic Warp Tunnel: A dimensional star-streak tunnel plunges the camera through a lunar crater directly into the Sea of Tranquility.

- Mechanical Exploded Breakdown: The Apollo Lunar Module Eagle separates dynamically along mechanical axes into 7 distinct assemblies (Ascent stage and cabin, docking drogue, egress ladder, RCS thruster quads, propellant tanks, landing gear, and descent engine chassis), accompanied by real-time 3D telemetry tags.

- Lunar Surface Archaeology: Visitors explore Tranquility Base and Hadley–Apennine on the lunar surface, inspecting the Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR), Passive Seismic Experiment (PSE), and Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV).

- Continuous Infinite Loop: An orbital Earthrise pulls the viewer back into space and smoothly returns to the morning of launch, symbolizing the perpetual loop of human exploration.

2. WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- Demystifies Aerospace Engineering: Rather than looking at flat photos or static diagrams, users interactively see how multi-stage rockets and lunar landers are physically put together and deployed.

- Preserves Lunar Cultural Heritage: Turns complex historical catalogs into an engaging, open digital museum accessible to anyone with an internet connection.

- Zero-Installation Universal Access: Runs directly inside modern web browsers on desktops, laptops, tablets, and phones without needing app downloads or special hardware.

- Highlights Active Space Science: Shows the public that artifacts left on the Moon are not just historical relics; the Apollo 11 Laser Retroreflector is still actively pinged by Earth-based observatories today to measure the lunar orbit.

3. WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT?

- Inspiring the Artemis Generation: Connecting Apollo's historic footprints directly to what is waiting on the Moon today builds excitement and awareness for NASA's upcoming Artemis missions.

- Extraterrestrial Archaeology Awareness: Promotes the global recognition and preservation of historic lunar landing sites under heritage agreements.

- Educational Value: Provides teachers, students, and space enthusiasts with an intuitive, turnkey visual tool combining history, physics, and spacecraft architecture.

4. WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

- Coding Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language for custom rocket flame and turbulence shaders), HTML5, CSS3.

- 3D Graphics Engine: Three.js, React Three Fiber, React Three Drei, WebGL 2.0 with ACES Filmic color grading.

- 3D Optimization: Google Draco 3D geometry compression to shrink 3D model file sizes by over 70% for fast loading.

- Motion and Scroll Orchestration: GSAP (GreenSock), ScrollTrigger, and Lenis inertia physics for smooth 60 FPS scrolling.

- Audio Engine: Web Audio API for synthesized multi-track rocket rumble, space drones, and thruster sound effects, paired with Web Speech synthesis narration.

- Data Sources: NASA 3D Resources, NASA Apollo Flight Journal, NSSDCA/COSPAR master catalog IDs, and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) elevation maps.

- Development Tools: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Node.js.

5. HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

- Continuous Infinite Narrative Loop: The entire mission runs in one unbroken 3D camera timeline that seamlessly connects Earth, orbit, lunar surface, and Earthrise back to the launch pad without traditional page reloads or cutscenes.

- Broadsheet Newspaper Match-Cut: Bridges vintage 1969 print journalism typography with interactive WebGL, transforming static historical news into live 3D exploration.

- Igloo-Style Spatial Telemetry: Incorporates futuristic radial guidance rings, crosshairs, and floating 3D information badges anchored directly into the lunar regolith.

- Staged Kinematic Explosion: Instead of blowing parts outward randomly, components separate in calibrated engineering order along realistic structural axes.

6. WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

- Performance and Device Support: Clamped device pixel ratio between 1.0 and 1.5, used local clipping planes, and culled off-screen scenes so complex 3D assets run smoothly at 60 FPS without overheating mobile devices or budget GPUs.

- Archival and Historical Accuracy: Grounded all artifact details in official NASA records, including exact landing coordinates, dry masses, COSPAR IDs, and operational lifespans.

- Honest Curatorial Labeling: Clearly distinguished verified external geometry from unmodeled interior systems to preserve historical integrity.

- User Experience and Accessibility: Built in sound volume controls, mute toggles, orbit inspection controls, keyboard navigation, and responsive layouts for all screen sizes.
